cim: Forward Amsterdam - Key Event Insights & Recap
cim_eredeti: Forward Amsterdam - Key Event Insights & Recap
szoveg_eredeti:
Surrounded by centuries of Dutch masters at Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum on 5 November 2026, supply chain leaders gathered for Flexport Forward to tackle a central question: what happens when artificial intelligence takes the wheel of global trade?

Global trade is heading for a record year, yet nearly $2 trillion is still lost to supply chain waste. To mark ten years in Europe, Flexport brought supply chain leaders to the Rijksmuseum to explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping global logistics.

Here is what stood out: artificial intelligence delivers when the data, the planning and the people behind it are ready. Read on for where artificial intelligence is already doing real work, why people still make it happen, what 2027 has in store, and how to plan for scenarios that feel a bit crazy. Three customers also share how they make decisions, and where their data still falls short.

Ryan Petersen, Flexport’s Chief Executive Officer and Founder, puts the waste in global supply chains at roughly $2 trillion, broken down into about $1.2 trillion a year in sales lost to stock-outs, $600 billion in inventory thrown away or heavily discounted, containers that average just 70% full, and unplanned air freight.

At their core, these are data and planning challenges. Flexport is betting that feeding real-time data into artificial intelligence will outperform static, quarterly spreadsheets. As these four real-world examples show:

Artificial intelligence now executes or heavily assists with about 75% of the work items needed to move a container door to door. Agents also monitor performance indicators and suggest new automations. For one European customer’s 10% invoice-discount rule, artificial intelligence writes the code and a person reviews it before it goes live.

Flexport rebuilt its shipment detail page to display every stock keeping unit and item. In customs, where the United States issued 53 tariff executive orders in 52 weeks in 2025, a ‘spell check’ artificial intelligence agent cut error rates in Flexport’s manual compliance reviews from 2% to 0.2%.

When customers place bookings, Flexport looks for ways to consolidate freight, cutting container counts by about 14% on average once consolidation is switched on. A person on the customer’s team still decides whether a shipment can arrive three days later to save $2,000, while Flexport Atlas displays carrier-published and Flexport-observed transit times side by side.

Flexport has launched its Model Context Protocol connector, allowing a customer’s own artificial intelligence tools to talk directly to Flexport. Users can add it as a connector in Claude, Copilot or ChatGPT to track shipments, get bookable quotes and book freight without opening the platform. Flexport plans to add more services and data every few months.

Flexport sees its role as a trusted layer between decisions made by artificial intelligence and action in the physical world, and that layer relies on people on the ground.

The doorman fallacy: A hotel chain that automates its doorman saves money on a spreadsheet, only to lose the greeting, the directions and the security that came with the role. The same risk applies when companies rush to automate jobs without seeing everything those roles hold together.

Offices on the ground: Local teams bring the customer relationships, procurement expertise and exception handling that keep goods moving. Flexport’s European network continues to expand: Paris is up and running, Dublin opens in the first quarter of 2027, and Turkey and Poland are on the way.

The artificial intelligence accelerator: Flexport’s internal training programme teaches about 160 employees per quarter, just under 10% of the workforce, to build with artificial intelligence. Participants spend one day a week for 13 weeks in the programme, finishing with a project that automates part of their own daily work.

AI is perfect for the industry. The industry is perfect for AI.

Artificial intelligence only delivers if the plan around it holds up, and 2027 will put those plans to the test. Chris Rogers, S&P Global’s Head of Supply Chain Research and a Flexport alum, joined Flexport President Sanne Manders on stage and predicted a similar level of disruption next year. Trade volumes remain on track for a record high, up about 3%, buoyed by strong consumer spending and the artificial intelligence boom. Meanwhile, S&P Global’s monthly survey of 27,000 companies shows supplier delivery times are starting to recover.

Still, six major bottlenecks will carry over from 2026:

S&P Global expects the Middle East conflict to persist over a 12-month horizon with no clear off-ramp. Security around the Suez Canal remains a serious concern, and Houthi attacks are not expected to stop.

As the conflict continues, supply networks have adapted. Machinery imports into Ukraine now exceed 2018 levels, with more deliveries arriving by land than by sea.

Low river levels at Kaub on the Rhine continue to disrupt barge shipments. Similar patterns are appearing on the Mississippi and in Latin America, and inland waterway constraints are expected to persist.

Cost-of-living pressures are keeping labour tensions high. Isolated strike risks in 2027 sit in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Canada, while on the United States West Coast, just two dozen port watchmen could stop the gates from opening.

Semiconductor prices are back near pandemic highs, and S&P Global expects that pricing pressure to continue through 2027, impacting anyone buying electronics or memory.

A single malicious email link recently took a major automaker offline for two months and its suppliers for three. S&P Global is watching closely for a catastrophic infrastructure hack next year.

Resilience is always treated as a luxury. This year has taught us that it just can't be.

Head of Supply Chain Research, S&P Global

Plans rarely survive the year intact: what Rogers expects in January has never matched how the year actually unfolds. His rule is to plan for the scenarios that feel a bit out there. Ask which core assumption could break your plan, and build around that. One company, for example, asked its wood buyer for the worst disruption he had ever seen: ash trees dying back in the United Kingdom. Their next question was simple: what if pine did the same across Europe?

To prepare, Rogers and Manders recommend asking ‘what if?’ and getting everyone who owns a piece of the supply chain into the same room. Manders suggests listing the slightly crazy scenarios and keeping the chief financial officer informed.

Waiting is the most common planning mistake. S&P Global began its 2027 planning in mid-2026 and is already urging leaders to start conversations around 2028.

One northern European company had 25 procurement teams, 25 risk managers and a chief financial officer in every division, with nobody talking in the same room. Simply bringing them together surfaced critical vulnerabilities before any artificial intelligence was deployed.

Carrying inventory is expensive, and companies are shifting from asking about ‘China plus one’ to ‘China or plus one’. Adding a second supplier can hurt unit economics, but so can holding an extra million euros in excess stock.

I think 2027 is going to be a watershed where the digital haves and have-nots are really going to see differences in performance.

Head of Supply Chain Research, S&P Global

Lorenzo Favetta, Flexport’s General Manager for Benelux, hosted a panel with the head of logistics at a fashion retailer, the supply chain procurement manager at a healthcare product company and the logistics lead at a mobility manufacturer. Asked about 2027, most of the room expected it to be at least as disruptive as 2026.
